To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inflammation-induced neurodegeneration of Multiple Sclerosis involves a mitochondrionaffecting mechanism.

1) mitochondrial dysfunction may contribute to the neurodegenerative component of Multiple Sclerosis; 2) this mitochondrial mechanism may be linked to the immune response; 3) the mechanism involves a mitochondrial DNA mutation; and 4) the mitochondrial dysfunction is associated with a specific clinical phenotype of Multiple Sclerosis.
mitochondrial abnormalities are a key feature of MS and that these abnormalities are likely to be involved in neurodegeneration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how neurodegeneration develops in the course of MS.
the development of new strategies to halt or prevent the degenerative process in MS, which may be achieved by the development of new drugs or by the use of existing agents in new ways.
understanding the pathogenesis of MS, with particular attention to the degenerative components of tissue injury, and the development of novel strategies to counteract these processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MS is a neurodegenerative disorder with an inflammatory component.
MS is a neurodegenerative disorder, which involves both inflammation and degeneration.
the neurodegeneration in progressive MS is a multifactorial process, which is initiated by the inflammatory response and involves a mitochondrionaffecting component.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mitochondrial component in MS is not only a secondary phenomenon, but also a major determinant of neurodegeneration.
mitochondrial dysfunction is an important factor in the development of neurodegeneration, but the mechanism is not fully elucidated.
the inflammation-induced neurodegeneration in the MS brain and spinal cord is partly independent from demyelination, and that the mitochondrial mechanism of cell-death may be involved in the process.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mitochondrial dysfunction may be a key factor in neurodegeneration in the context of MS and that mitochondrial dysfunction is not limited to the oligodendrocytes, as it is often thought, but is present in other cells as well, including neurons and astrocytes.
the mitochondrion is the final common pathway in neurodegeneration, and the inflammatory process is likely to induce mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death.
the mitochondrial mechanism of neurodegeneration, although not yet proven to be the main cause of neurodegeneration is a possible cause and should be further studied.
